## Abstract

Estimating time-since-discharge from passive sensing is valuable in low-visibility operations, where misidentification carries a high cost. We model post-discharge thermal decay in firearm components through Newton’s Law of Cooling, enabling threat assessment without active illumination or contact. Using an MSX-enhanced homography to align thermal and RGB domains, we fit decay profiles for two structurally distinct platforms. The Glock 17 satisfies the Lumped Capacitance assumption and yields consistent exponential fits, whereas the Rossi Puma violates it, delimiting the method’s domain of validity. A probabilistic hypothesis test then converts a single temperature measurement into a statistically grounded lower bound on shot count.
